title: The Six Trillion Dollar Man
gist: Gavekal argues the north star of US policymaking is keeping US equity prices high, citing Trump's 'stocks up, oil down' remark after signing the Iran memorandum of understanding in Versailles, implying US adversaries gain more leverage by hitting the Nasdaq than military assets. Amid market turbulence, the firm falls back on its framework that three prices (energy, 10-year US treasury yields, and the US dollar) determine long-term asset-price direction and relative calls such as growth vs value and EM vs DM.

themes.theme: Equity prices as the US policy north star

insights.claim: Gavekal argues the north star of US policymaking is first and foremost keeping US equity prices high, a dynamic it says was visible again on Monday (Beat Notz's dictum).
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Policy responses can be expected to lean toward supporting equity markets when they fall, acting as an implicit backstop.

insights.claim: Gavekal contends that adversaries in a conflict with the US would gain more leverage by causing major Nasdaq losses than by destroying battleships, jet planes or soldiers, because equity losses are far more likely to change US policy.

insights.so_what: US equity markets become a geopolitical pressure point, raising the strategic vulnerability of tech-heavy indices in conflicts.

insights.claim: Gavekal holds that over the long term three prices determine the direction of asset prices: the price of energy, the price of capital (the 10-year US treasury yield) and the price of the US dollar.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Macro allocation calls can be anchored on directional views of oil/energy, long-end yields and the dollar.
insights.quote: These three prices are the price of energy, the price of capital (as measured by the yield on 10-year US treasuries) and the price of the US dollar.
